title: Cursive Oracle Completion Charter
objective: Complete the CursiveOracle work by fixing compiler conformance bugs exposed by
the oracle at the compiler source of truth, then resume oracle foundation work
only after the compiler can correctly execute the required Cursive constructs.
primaryAuthorityAndWorkProduct: This charter has one primary work product:
CursiveOracle/
The oracle is the project being built. `docs/CursiveSpecification.md` is the
only source of truth for expected language behavior. The oracle must derive its
model, obligations, generated cases, expected diagnostics, runtime expectations,
and coverage ledger from the real specification text and formal content.
`HelloCursive/` is not the oracle, not a substitute oracle, and not a source of
expected behavior. It is only a compiler regression harness that may be used
after a `CursiveOracle/` failure has been traced to a compiler implementation
bug in a spec-supported construct.
Do not derive any oracle expectation from:
`HelloCursive/` project behavior;
the legacy external auditing table;
trace labels in compiler source;
generated conformance label registries;
current compiler behavior;
fixture names, filenames, or exact strings from a failing case.
The required direction of evidence is:

docs/CursiveSpecification.md -> CursiveOracle reference model / obligation / expectation -> compiler-under-test execution through public compiler/runtime entry points -> ComparisonResult and coverage ledger
The allowed temporary diagnostic direction for compiler blockers is:
CursiveOracle failure -> specific spec-supported construct -> canonical compiler owner -> focused HelloCursive regression, if useful -> compiler fix -> CursiveOracle passes farther
successCriteria: CursiveOracle check/build/executable entry points are the driver for the current task and pass before claiming oracle foundation work complete.
Compiler fixes are made in canonical compiler modules, not in oracle source, when the oracle exposes a compiler bug.

Focused HelloCursive regressions may exercise the exposed construct through public compiler build and executable entry points, but only as lock-in for a compiler fix already justified by the spec and oracle failure.
Oracle expectations are derived from the parsed spec and reference model, not from compiler labels, trace output, HelloCursive, or the external audit table.
No placeholders, shims, fallback paths, test-name branches, or oracle rewrites hide compiler non-conformance.

No hand-authored oracle file is added merely to mirror the intended tree. A new module/file is allowed only when the same task implements real behavior, tests it through CursiveOracle, and wires it into the existing module graph.

The oracle has a single, oracle-wide output and verbose logging system. Every phase uses that system for progress, failure context, evidence paths, verbose trace events, and final summaries; no phase returns a bare status code or writes one-off ad hoc diagnostics.

Oracle failures are self-identifying before debug tracing is needed: every nonzero oracle run emits the current phase, suite/case/check or obligation id, failure classification, expected/observed values when available, relevant spec unit or blocker classification, and the artifact or command that produced the evidence.
antiDriftExecutionGates: Before any non-control write, answer these questions from the current evidence:
1. What exact CursiveOracle failure, missing oracle capability, or spec-derived obligation is this edit advancing?
2. What exact spec section, formal rule, grammar block, diagnostic row, or normative sentence authorizes the expected behavior?
3. What is the canonical owner of this behavior?
4. Is this edit in that owner, or is it only a regression/verification artifact explicitly allowed by this charter?
5. Does this edit leave any shim, fallback, compatibility path, placeholder, duplicate implementation, test-only branch, or fixture-specific special case?
6. What command will verify this change through CursiveOracle?
If any answer is missing, do not edit code. Inspect the spec, oracle, compiler,
or existing module graph until the answer is concrete.
Task execution must follow this order:
1. Reproduce the current CursiveOracle check/build/run state.
2. Read the relevant `docs/CursiveSpecification.md` section before deciding what behavior is expected.
3. Classify the issue:
oracle missing capability;
compiler non-conformance;
runtime non-conformance;
unsupported-by-current-oracle blocker;
outside-conformance / informative spec text.
4. Edit only the canonical owner for that classification.
5. Use HelloCursive only for a narrow compiler regression when classification is compiler non-conformance.
6. Re-run CursiveOracle check/build/run and record whether it advances.
Oracle output and failure logging gate:
1. Main must initialize one oracle output/logging context and pass it through every oracle phase instead of letting phases write ad hoc output.

2. The oracle is always verbose. Do not add verbosity toggles, environment variables, config switches, quiet modes, or trace/summary mode selection. Conformance failures must be diagnosable from every normal oracle run.
3. Every phase boundary must log phase begin, phase end, status, elapsed/order marker when available, and summary counts relevant to that phase.
4. A CursiveOracle executable failure must identify the last entered phase, suite/case/check or obligation id, and source owner before returning a nonzero status.
5. Assertion-style oracle failures must print the expected value, observed value, failure kind, and canonical owner that should be inspected next.

6. Spec ingestion failures must print the spec path, byte/line/span position when known, parsed section/unit context, and whether the issue is a spec parse error obligation or an oracle parser defect.
7. Reference-model failures must print selected obligation ids, source spec spans, expected semantic rule/model owner, and unsupported/outside-conformance classification when applicable.
8. Compiler invocation failures must print the compiler command, compiler exit status, diagnostic artifact path, stdout/stderr artifact paths, and selected obligation ids when those exist.

9. Runtime executable failures must print the runtime command, runtime exit status or panic code when observable, stdout/stderr artifact paths, and the associated ComparisonResult when that layer exists.
10. Comparison failures must print case id, obligation ids, mismatch kind, expected summary, observed summary, spec span, and evidence paths.
11. Coverage failures must print coverage counts by state and top blockers with obligation id, source span, state, and blocker reason.

12. Output must be emitted through the spec-defined capability surface `ctx.fs~>write_stdout` / `ctx.fs~>write_stderr`; do not add a host wrapper or external script as the oracle's reporting mechanism.
13. When output support itself fails, preserve the original failure status and include that reporting failure in the nearest available report artifact rather than masking the oracle failure.
14. Direct calls to `write_stdout` and `write_stderr` are owned by `Core::Reporting` only. Other oracle modules emit typed reporting records through the output context.

15. `Core::Reporting` owns the event-line protocol validator and output-regression artifact writer. `Suites::SelfTest` is the initial caller that proves the protocol without turning selftests into conformance truth.

16. Output verification must check field order, field presence, escaping, and typed vocabularies. Loose substring checks are acceptable only as additional smoke evidence after the protocol validator has proven the event line shape.
If a compiler regression is added under `HelloCursive/`, it must name the
language construct under test, avoid oracle-specific names, include both positive
and negative/control behavior where applicable, and be verified only as a
regression for the compiler fix. Passing `HelloCursive/` never satisfies an
oracle task by itself.
If the oracle cannot yet express a spec obligation, the correct next task is to
build the missing oracle module under `CursiveOracle/`, not to encode that
obligation as ad hoc string matching in a test harness.
sourceTreeContract: The source tree is a planning contract, not a placeholder checklist. Entries use

path: <repo-relative path> module: <Cursive assembly/module path, or n/a for non-source paths> status: existing | planned | fixture-input | generated-output phase: <implementation phase or gate> role: <manifest | docs | canonical-owner | suite | fixture | output> responsibility: <owned behavior> files:
<file name>: <owned declarations / behavior> allowed-when: <condition that authorizes creating or editing the entry> forbidden:
Cursive module identity is directory-based. A directory containing `.cursive` files is one module, and all `.cursive` files in that directory share that module.
`Cursive.toml` must list only assembly roots that exist and contain real `.cursive` files.

Planned entries are not write authority. A planned file may be created only when the same task implements real behavior in that file, wires it into `CursiveOracle`, and verifies it through the oracle entry point.
Do not create empty directories, TODO-only files, placeholder modules, facade shells, truth tables, or mirrored hierarchy buckets.
Build artifacts under `CursiveOracle/build/**` are generated compiler output and are excluded from the source tree contract.

incrementally, only when the active task implements the named behavior with real
types/procedures and verifies it through `CursiveOracle`.

requiredBehavior: The oracle has one canonical output/logging subsystem used by every oracle phase.
The subsystem is always verbose and has no verbosity toggles, quiet modes, trace modes, summary modes, environment variables, or configuration switches.

Oracle mode, phase selection, output behavior, and test selection must not depend on environment variables, host process state, wrapper scripts, or hidden external configuration. Every normal oracle executable run must follow the Cursive-owned source/project state visible through the repository and the explicit Cursive call graph.
Every normal oracle run emits enough phase, checkpoint, failure, evidence, and summary information to diagnose failures without rerunning in another mode.
The output subsystem defines typed event, failure, evidence, and summary records for the full oracle pipeline.

The subsystem defines a deterministic rendered line protocol before implementation. Each emitted line must be derived from a typed record and must include stable fields rather than free-form prose as the primary diagnostic contract.

The minimum line fields are: protocol, run_scope, event_index, event_kind, severity, phase, subject_kind, subject_id, owner, status, failure_kind, evidence_kind, expected, observed, evidence_path, metric_kind, metric_value, and message.
The initial protocol name is `cursive-oracle-event-v1`.

The normal executable run started from `Main.cursive` uses exactly `run_scope=main.default` for every event line. Output-regression artifacts use exactly `run_scope=output_regression.<scenario>`, where `<scenario>` is the artifact basename listed in this charter. A later source-level entry procedure may add a new run scope only by updating this charter in the same task; it must not be selected by environment variables, host process state, wrappers, or hidden configuration.
`event_index` is a monotonically increasing run-local integer carried by the output context so repeated phase/checkpoint names remain ordered and distinguishable.

The line protocol is ordered key-value text. Field order is exactly: `protocol`, `run_scope`, `event_index`, `event_kind`, `severity`, `phase`, `subject_kind`, `subject_id`, `owner`, `status`, `failure_kind`, `evidence_kind`, `expected`, `observed`, `evidence_path`, `metric_kind`, `metric_value`, `message`.

Rendered event lines use single-space-separated `key=value` fields in that exact order. There is no optional field reordering and no alternative JSON, CSV, table, or prose line format for the primary diagnostic stream.
Every field is present on every rendered event line. Fields without a value render as `-`, not as an omitted key.
Field values are ASCII event metadata unless the field explicitly carries spec text or source excerpts in a later task. Spec text and source excerpts must preserve UTF-8 exactly when emitted.

Field values must not contain raw newline characters or raw field separators. `Core::Reporting` owns a single value escaping helper with these exact rules: encode the UTF-8 bytes `%`, space, tab, carriage return, newline, `=`, `,`, `|`, `\`, `[`, and `]` as uppercase percent escapes (`%25`, `%20`, `%09`, `%0D`, `%0A`, `%3D`, `%2C`, `%7C`, `%5C`, `%5B`, `%5D`). Preserve all other valid UTF-8 bytes exactly. A present empty value renders as `%00`. A present literal single hyphen renders as `%2D` so `-` remains reserved for absent fields only.

Lists, including obligation ids and evidence paths, render as `[escaped-item,escaped-item]` using the same value escaping helper for each item. A present empty list renders as `[]`. An absent list-valued field still renders as `-`.
Each rendered line ends with exactly one newline.
Free-form `message` text is secondary; the primary diagnostic contract is the typed fields above.
Counts and summary numbers must use typed `metric_kind` and `metric_value` fields, not prose-only text.
`severity` values are exactly: `info`, `warning`, `error`, and `fatal`.
